title: Kinsey
full_review:
When Alfred Kinsey published his seminal study, "Sexual Behavior in the Human Male," in 1948, one commentator likened its effect to that of the atom bomb. More than 50 years later, another mushroom cloud is poised to explode over writer-director Bill Condon's controversial, sexually graphic new biopic, "Kinsey" (Fox Searchlight), starring Liam Neeson in the title role.

The movie will likely generate strong reactions from both those who admire Kinsey as a courageous crusader and those who consider him a degenerate.

Defenders will view the picture as a sober portrait of the man credited with emancipating sex from the shackles of Puritanism. Conversely, critics will question not only the movie's accuracy, but the appropriateness of celebrating a man whom many blame for jump-starting the sexual revolution by redefining societal mores and jettisoning inhibition and traditional morality to the relic heap of Victorian prudery.

Much like Kinsey's nonjudgmental attitude toward sex, Condon approaches his subject with a fair degree of objectivity, painting him in neither overly hagiographic nor villainous shades.
The film chronicles Kinsey's life, beginning with his strict upbringing in a religious household headed by his authoritarian Methodist father (John Lithgow).

Rebelling against his father's rigid piety and drawn to nature, Kinsey becomes a Harvard-educated zoologist -- and foremost expert in gall wasps -- eventually landing a biology post at the University of Indiana, where he meets and marries free-thinking grad student Clara McMillen (Laura Linney).

Prompted by his students' naivete regarding sexual matters, he decides to teach a "marriage course" where sexuality can be discussed openly in frank terms.

Appalled by the dearth of reliable data on sex, Kinsey undertakes a pioneering study of sexual behavior from a strictly scientific point of view, crisscrossing the country to conduct thousands of interviews with people -- both heterosexual and homosexual -- to compile detailed sex histories, including those of prostitutes and sex offenders.

To assist him in the daunting task, he recruits a team of research fellows, including Wardell Pomeroy (Chris O'Donnell), Paul Gebhard (Timothy Hutton), and Clyde Martin (Peter Sarsgaard), a bisexual with whom both he and his wife have an affair.

Operating under the permissive principle that no deviant behavior is taboo so long as it is consensual, Kinsey encourages sexual experimentation among his coterie -- including spouse-swapping. But his trumpeting of free love ultimately backfires, fueling tensions within his tight-knit group.

Kinsey publishes his findings in 1948 to best-seller acclaim -- making the covers of magazines and winding up in the lyrics of a Cole Porter song -- but "red scare" fears turn the tide of popular opinion against him as he embarks on a follow-up study of female sexuality. His work is branded a communist plot to undermine American values, prompting his benefactors to pull their funding. Dejected, he is forced to seek new backers, hat in hand. A final scene concedes that love is not a statistic to be tallied and tabulated.

While not meriting an unconditional endorsement, the film has a lot going for it cinematically, including a handsome period look and a solid cast, anchored by Neeson's nuanced performance.
Condon's script presents a textured picture of a complex figure, though, as is usually the case with biographies which must telescope decades into hours, the story tends to emphasize chronology over character, offering little real insight into the man behind the obsession.

While stopping short of advocacy, the picture clearly casts the libido liberator in a sympathetic mold. Still, the film does not gloss over Kinsey's flaws, including his monomaniacal pursuit of knowledge at all cost and his blindness to the pain caused to those around him. It does, however, downplay some of the more unsavory allegations about his life, including his sadomasochistic tendencies and dubious methodology and accusations that he unethically obtained information from known pedophiles. The last charge does get cursory treatment during one interview scene.
Understandably, many Catholic viewers will find much of the film offensive, but Condon at least attempts to handle the subject matter with an eye toward serious exploration.

In watching "Kinsey," the overwhelming sensation is not one of salacious heat, but clinical coldness. By depersonalizing sex and divorcing biology from morality, Kinsey gutted the conjugal intimacy of love, and in doing so reduced men and women to the stature of glorified gall wasps. Viewers are left with an impression of Kinsey not as an evil avatar of hedonism, but as a pathetic individual incapable of comprehending the sacred splendor of human sexuality, like a man who spends his whole life studying colors, but can never appreciate a sunset.

Because of a relativistic view of sexual morality, explicit sexual images, including graphic straight and gay sexual encounters, full frontal nudity, several masturbation scenes, candid sexual discussions and recurring rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
